Purpose: Establish whose deck this is, for whom, and when — the slide that stays on screen while people settle in.
What goes on it: Client name, project descriptor, both logos, date, a hero image or looping render of the space.
Required inputs / assets: Client name; project name; date; client logo
Optional inputs: Hero image or hero video; accent colour pulled from the logo
Notes: Accent colour should already be derived from the client logo at project creation.

Purpose: Tell the room how long this will take and when their part comes up, so nobody interrupts early.
What goes on it: 5-7 numbered sections matching the deck's own section dividers, with an approximate timing.
Notes: Generate from the sections actually present after rules run — never hardcode.

Purpose: Establish that the firm can carry a project of this size before any design opinion is offered.
What goes on it: Positioning line, what we do end-to-end, scale markers, delivery footprint.
Optional inputs: Founding year; office locations; team size
Notes: Auto-populate from the brand profile — this is the brand-driven auto-population ask.

Purpose: Convert the claim in the previous slide into figures that can be checked.
What goes on it: 3-4 stats: sq ft delivered, projects completed, cities, average handover variance.
Notes: Filter to the project's own typology where the data supports it — a GCC client wants GCC numbers.

Purpose: Borrow credibility from recognisable names, especially ones in the same typology.
What goes on it: A grid of 12-24 client logos, ideally sorted so same-typology clients lead.
Notes: GAP: no logo-wall layout. A grid layout is needed; freeform works but every logo must be placed by hand.

Purpose: Put names and faces to the people the client will actually deal with.
What goes on it: 4-8 people: photo, name, role, one line of relevant experience.
Notes: GAP: no team-grid layout. freeform can do it but is manual.

Purpose: Answer the unspoken comparison against the two other firms pitching this week.
What goes on it: 3-5 differentiators, each one line, converging on a single outcome statement.
Notes: Differentiators should be typology-specific — 'we do GCCs' beats 'we are detail-oriented'.

Purpose: Show one comparable project in enough depth to be believed, rather than ten in a blur.
What goes on it: One project: brief, what was solved, 2-3 images, outcome figure.
Notes: Pick by typology match first, then by scale. Same-typology beats same-city.

Purpose: Mark the shift from credentials to the client's own project.
What goes on it: Numeral, section title, one-line framing question.
Notes: Reuses pillarSectionSlide() in src/lib/conceptSlides.ts.

Purpose: Repeat the brief back in the client's own words — the cheapest way to prove you listened and to surface a misunderstanding while it is still free.
What goes on it: What was asked for, the constraints given, the success criteria, in the client's phrasing.
Notes: Quote the client verbatim where possible. Paraphrase reads as interpretation.

Purpose: Put every number the whole room must agree on in one place, early.
What goes on it: Area, headcount, floors, location, target handover, budget band.
Notes: If any figure here is wrong, everything downstream is wrong. Present it for confirmation.

Purpose: Extract the client's visual and cultural vocabulary so later design moves can be traced back to it rather than to taste.
What goes on it: Brand palette, logo usage, tone, product/service imagery, existing spatial cues.
Notes: The E-Com Express reference slide is exactly this pattern — see ECOM_SLIDE_2_ELEMENTS.

Purpose: Name what the client wants the workplace to do for them, in their words, before proposing how.
Suggested title: What do you aspire for at your workplace?
What goes on it: 6-8 aspiration statements as cards or icons, drawn from the briefing or a staff survey.
Optional inputs: Staff survey results; leadership interview quotes
Notes: Pattern exists as ECOM_SLIDE_1_ELEMENTS. Survey-backed statements carry far more weight than assumed ones.

Purpose: Make the abstract headcount into specific people with different needs, so the space mix has a defence.
What goes on it: 4-6 personas orbiting a core: photo, role, work pattern, what they need from the space.
Notes: The orbit layout was built for exactly this.

Purpose: Show that one desk type cannot serve the whole organisation — the argument every varied setting later depends on.
What goes on it: The split across focused / collaborative / social / hybrid / mobile / meeting-heavy, with percentages.
Notes: State plainly whether the split is measured or assumed — clients notice, and assumed splits get challenged.

Purpose: Fix the number the plan is sized against, and the growth it must absorb without a rebuild.
What goes on it: Current headcount, day-one, year-3 and year-5 projections, per department.
Notes: Growth assumptions belong on the slide, not in the appendix. They are the whole basis of the area.

Purpose: Justify any desk-sharing ratio with observed data instead of an assertion.
Suggested title: How full is the office, really?
What goes on it: Attendance by day of week, peak vs average occupancy, historic utilisation, the ratio it supports.
Notes: Without real data do not propose a sharing ratio. An unbacked ratio is the fastest way to lose the room.

Purpose: Walk the client through a day in the space so gaps are noticed before they are built.
What goes on it: Arrival, orientation, work, meetings, breaks, social, departure — as a sequence.
Optional inputs: Per-stage pain points from the current office
Notes: Strongest when contrasted against the pain points of the current office.

Purpose: Calibrate expectations against comparable workplaces before proposing anything.
What goes on it: 3-4 comparable projects with the metric that matters — density, ratio, cost or area per person.
Notes: Benchmarks must match typology and city to be credible.

Purpose: Close the understanding section with the agreed brief — the thing the rest of the deck answers.
What goes on it: Left: the constraints and givens. Right: the objectives design must deliver.
Notes: Get explicit agreement here. Every later disagreement traces back to a skipped sign-off on this slide.

Purpose: Mark the shift from brief to the physical building.
What goes on it: Numeral, section title, framing question.

Purpose: Place the office in its city and building, and surface what the location gives and costs.
What goes on it: Locus map, a reveal photo of the building/floor, address, compass and sun path.
Notes: The site-locus layout already has the hover-reveal and compass built in.

Purpose: Show the plate everyone will be reasoning about: core position, column grid, depth, glazing.
What goes on it: Annotated plate with core, columns, structural grid, glazing lines and floor-to-ceiling height.
Required inputs / assets: Floor plan from the landlord or survey
Notes: Set `visual: 'image'` so the plan fills the right half rather than the generated diagram.

Purpose: Record what is there now — the baseline for a refurbishment, and the evidence for what must go.
What goes on it: Survey photos on a key plan, each hotspot opening the photos for that area.
Notes: Use hotspots with galleries so each area's photos open in place. Mandatory for refurbishment, meaningless for greenfield.

Purpose: State honestly what the building will not allow, next to what it uniquely offers — credibility comes from naming both.
What goes on it: Left: constraints (core position, low ceiling, single access, services). Right: opportunities (aspect, terrace, height, daylight).
Notes: Naming constraints early makes the later plan read as resolution rather than compromise.

Purpose: Justify where the open plan and the enclosed rooms go, using the sun rather than preference.
What goes on it: Sun path across the plate, glare risk zones, the daylight-driven planning rule that follows.
Notes: The planning rule is the point: perimeter for people, core for rooms — or the reasoned exception.

Purpose: Confirm what the base build provides so later MEP scope is not a surprise.
What goes on it: HVAC provision, power availability, fire systems, lift and washroom cores, what the fit-out must add.
Notes: Insufficient base-build capacity is the most common late cost shock — flag any shortfall here, in writing.

Purpose: Mark the shift from analysis to proposal.
What goes on it: Numeral, section title, framing question.

Purpose: Show that the design follows a repeatable method, not inspiration — this is what de-risks the commission.
What goes on it: The six steps — Understand, Analyse, Strategise, Design, Test, Resolve — converging on a resolved workplace.
Optional inputs: Client-side milestones mapped onto each step
Notes: designSequenceSlide() in src/lib/conceptSlides.ts already builds this from DESIGN_SEQUENCE.

Purpose: State the single governing idea in one sentence, full-bleed, so the rest of the deck can be judged against it.
What goes on it: One sentence. No supporting points, no image competing with it.
Optional inputs: A background image at low opacity
Notes: If it needs two sentences it is not yet a concept. Rewrite until it fits in one.

Purpose: Unpack the big idea into the handful of moves that deliver it.
What goes on it: Lead line, 3-5 scannable points, one supporting visual.
Notes: This is the standard conceptSlide() shape — lead plus points plus image slot.

Purpose: Set the visual register before any specific room is shown, so renders land as expected rather than as a surprise.
What goes on it: 9-12 reference images in a grid: material, light, texture, spatial character.
Optional inputs: Per-image caption naming what it is being referenced for
Notes: GAP: no image-grid layout. freeform works but every image is placed by hand.

Purpose: Bridge from the client's brand and aspirations to the design language, so the leap is visible and traceable.
What goes on it: Keywords paired with the aspiration and brand element each one derives from.
Notes: Pattern exists as ECOM_SLIDE_3_ELEMENTS — explicitly the 'bringing aspiration and brand together' slide.

Purpose: Let the client see the concept against the alternative, and choose rather than merely accept.
What goes on it: Two treatments of the same space, revealed by a draggable slider.
Notes: Also the right layout for refurbishment before/after.

Purpose: Give the client a short rulebook they can hold later decisions against.
What goes on it: 4-6 principles, one line each, written as testable rules.
Notes: Write them so a later decision can actually fail one. 'Daylight for people, core for rooms' passes that test; 'thoughtful design' does not.

Purpose: Name the operating model — assigned, shared, activity-based or hybrid — because everything downstream depends on it.
What goes on it: The chosen model, the ratio it implies, what it requires of people and of technology.
Notes: Any model other than fully-assigned needs a change-management commitment on this slide, or it will not survive contact with staff.

Purpose: Fix the repeatable components once, so the plan is consistent and the BOQ is predictable.
What goes on it: Workstation sizes, cabin grades, room types, with dimensions and quantities.
Notes: Essential for GCCs conforming to a global standard and for operators repeating a centre format.

Purpose: Show where each concept move actually lands on the plan, so the concept reads as a plan and not as a poster.
What goes on it: Key plan with hotspots; each opens the concept driving that space.
Notes: Use ViewHotspot.spaceDetail.concept — this is precisely what the space-detail overlay was built for.

Purpose: Mark the shift from idea to plan.
What goes on it: Numeral, section title, framing question.

Purpose: Account for every square foot — the slide procurement and finance will actually read.
What goes on it: Zone, space type, quantity, unit area, total area, percentage of the plate, with a grand total.
Notes: GAP: no standalone table layout. Today this rides on LinkedView.seatingZones, which forces it next to a plan.

Purpose: Show the floor resolved into zones before any furniture, so the logic is judged on its own.
What goes on it: Colour-coded zones over the plate, with the adjacency logic stated.
Notes: Use LinkedViewStage to switch between Zoning and Layout on one image — that is what stages are for.

Purpose: Justify what sits next to what, from interaction frequency rather than convenience.
What goes on it: Bubble or matrix diagram of departments, weighted by interaction frequency.
Notes: Strongest when backed by an actual interaction survey rather than an org chart.

Purpose: Show that people can move without walking through someone else's concentration.
What goes on it: Primary and secondary routes over the plan, with egress distances and pinch points.
Notes: Overlay egress compliance here and the fire-safety slide gets much shorter.

Purpose: Give the audience the reference plan every later slide will point back to.
What goes on it: The full plan, labelled, with a legend and north point.
Notes: This is the view every hotspot and key-plan crop later refers to. Establish it once, clearly.

Purpose: Prove the headcount actually fits, at real furniture dimensions.
What goes on it: Fully furnished plan with workstation counts per zone.
Notes: The count on this plan must match the area statement exactly. A mismatch is noticed immediately.

Purpose: Reconcile what was required against what was achieved, zone by zone — the number the client checks hardest.
What goes on it: Zone-grouped Area / Required / Achieved table beside the plan, hover-linked to the hotspots.
Required inputs / assets: Required and achieved counts per zone; key plan
Optional inputs: Notes per row; Excel import of the capacity sheet
Notes: Fully built: LinkedView.seatingZones with two-way hover, plus Excel import via parseSeatingWorkbook.

Purpose: Explain the desk mix and the sharing ratio in one place, with the data behind it.
What goes on it: Counts by workstation type, the sharing ratio, and sq ft per person.
Notes: Tie the ratio back to the attendance slide, or it reads as an assumption.

Purpose: Show the meeting rooms were sized from meeting patterns, not from habit.
What goes on it: Rooms by capacity band, seats-per-head ratio, the booking data behind it.
Notes: Calendar data almost always shows too many large rooms and too few 2-4 person ones. Say so.

Purpose: Resolve which department sits on which floor before anyone argues about desks.
What goes on it: Floor-by-floor department allocation with headcount per floor.
Notes: Only meaningful for multi-floor projects — suppress it entirely on single-floor ones.

Purpose: Let the client interrogate the plan live — click any space and see the concept, render and occupancy that justify it.
What goes on it: Key plan with a hotspot per space; each opens concept, renders, walkthrough and occupancy.
Optional inputs: Per-zone walkthrough video; concept summary; BOQ note
Notes: Fully built: ViewHotspot.spaceDetail plus SpaceDetailOverlay. The strongest live-pitch moment in the product.

Purpose: Mark the shift from plan to experience.
What goes on it: Numeral, section title, framing question.

Purpose: Show the first thirty seconds of the building — the only space every visitor will judge.
What goes on it: Hero render, arrival sequence, reception desk, branding, seating, security interface.
Optional inputs: Material callouts; a second angle; branding detail
Notes: Always the strongest render in the deck. If only one image is ready, it should be this one.

Purpose: Show where visitors wait, and that waiting is not an afterthought.
What goes on it: Render, seating arrangement, refreshment provision, acoustic and visual separation from staff.
Notes: Escalate where the client suite is the commercial point of the office.

Purpose: Show where most people spend most of their time — the space the fit-out is really for.
What goes on it: Render, workstation type, desk spacing, storage, daylight access, acoustic treatment.
Optional inputs: Workstation detail; a second angle; dimensions
Notes: Show it at realistic occupancy. An empty workhall render invites doubt about whether it actually fits.

Purpose: Resolve the hierarchy question visually before it is negotiated person by person.
What goes on it: Render, cabin grades and sizes, glazing and privacy treatment, storage.
Notes: Show the grades as a published rule. Ad-hoc cabin sizing is where fit-out programmes go to die.

Purpose: Show the everyday rooms in the mix and the AV standard each one carries.
What goes on it: Renders of 2-3 room sizes, table configuration, AV, acoustic and glazing treatment.
Notes: State the AV standard per size band here and the technology slide gets much shorter.

Purpose: Show the room where the company's most consequential meetings happen.
What goes on it: Hero render, table, AV and video-conference setup, acoustic privacy, materiality.
Optional inputs: AV specification; a second angle; material detail
Notes: Usually the second-highest-value render after reception. Premium and above, it is mandatory.

Purpose: Show where calls happen, which is the single most common complaint in every open-plan office.
What goes on it: Render, quantity and distribution, acoustic rating, ventilation and power.
Notes: Quantity matters more than appearance. Give the booths-per-100-seat ratio explicitly.

Purpose: Show the informal settings that make the desk count defensible.
What goes on it: Render, settings variety, writable and display surfaces, power, acoustic zoning.
Notes: Escalates to mandatory under the Collaborative (ABW) concept — it is the concept's main evidence.

Purpose: Show the space that carries the most people per square foot and most of the social life.
What goes on it: Render, seating capacity, servery and pantry provision, peak-load sizing, dual use as town hall.
Optional inputs: Seating count; peak-load calculation; servery detail
Notes: Size for the peak sitting, not the average. Shift-based workplaces need the overlap number.

Purpose: Show where the whole office gathers, and prove the room can actually hold them.
What goes on it: Render, capacity in each configuration, AV and acoustics, operable partition strategy.
Notes: Multi-configuration capacity is the point. Show at least two layouts of the same room.

Purpose: Show the provision that signals the workplace takes care seriously — and which is often a statutory requirement.
What goes on it: Render, mother's room, quiet and prayer rooms, first aid, privacy and access control.
Notes: A mother's room is statutory at most Indian workplace sizes — check the threshold and state it.

Purpose: Show the provision, the fixture count and the accessibility compliance.
What goes on it: Render, fixture count against code, accessible provision, material and maintenance strategy.
Notes: Often landlord-provided. Include only where the fit-out actually covers it.

Purpose: Account for back-of-house so it is not discovered as a shortfall on site.
What goes on it: Print and copy, storage, lockers, housekeeping, UPS and server, with areas.
Notes: Under-provisioned back-of-house is the most common post-handover complaint. Give it real numbers.

Purpose: Show the specialist floor that drives the power, cooling, acoustic and compliance load of the whole project.
What goes on it: Render, desk configuration, screen arrangement, power and cooling, acoustic and recording compliance.
Optional inputs: Power and cooling load; compliance requirement
Notes: BFSI only. Services load here typically governs the entire electrical design.

Purpose: Show where office meets lab — the boundary that governs services, access and safety.
What goes on it: Render, transition and gowning zone, visual connection, services and access control boundary.
Notes: R&D, pharma and life sciences only. Confirm services capacity before committing to any adjacency.

Purpose: Show the production space that doubles as the brand's own set.
What goes on it: Render, shoot setup, lighting rig, acoustic treatment, edit suite adjacency, storage.
Optional inputs: Lighting and AV specification; acoustic ratings
Notes: Media, creative and D2C only. Acoustic isolation from the open plan is the hard part.

Purpose: Show the space that carries an operator's community programme and its events revenue.
What goes on it: Render, event configurations, capacity per setup, bar or servery, AV, after-hours access.
Notes: Managed-workspace operators only, where it is mandatory — it is a revenue line, not an amenity.

Purpose: Show the curated visitor journey that is the entire point of a showcase space.
What goes on it: Render, the visitor route, demo stations, AV and immersion, dwell times, reveal sequence.
Optional inputs: AV specification; content plan; dwell timings
Notes: Experience centres and innovation hubs only. Sequence carries more weight here than any single render.

Purpose: Show the 24x7 nerve centre and what running it around the clock demands.
What goes on it: Render, screen wall, desk configuration, shift handover space, 24x7 amenity provision.
Notes: E-commerce and logistics only. Size the amenities for shift overlap, not for headcount.

Purpose: Show where the public is received and served, and how they are kept separate from staff areas.
What goes on it: Render, counter arrangement, queuing and waiting, accessibility, staff-side separation.
Notes: Government, PSU and institutional only. Queue length and accessible counter height are the checkable items.

Purpose: Mark the shift from space to substance.
What goes on it: Numeral, section title, framing question.

Purpose: Fix what the workplace is made of, so renders can be trusted and the BOQ has a basis.
What goes on it: Material swatches with names, application, finish and maintenance note.
Notes: Name application per material. An unlabelled swatch board is decoration, not a specification.

Purpose: Fix the colour logic and its relationship to the client's brand.
What goes on it: Primary, secondary and accent colours, where each is applied, brand derivation.
Notes: Tie every colour back to the brand landscape slide, or it reads as arbitrary.

Purpose: Show the actual furniture, since it is what people touch and a large share of the budget.
What goes on it: Product images by category, with dimensions, finish and ergonomic specification.
Notes: Lead times belong here, not only on the programme slide — furniture is the usual critical path.

Purpose: Show the light, because it governs how every render will actually look when built.
What goes on it: Ambient, task and feature layers, fitting selection, lux levels, controls.
Notes: Lux targets per zone make this checkable rather than decorative.

Purpose: Show how the open plan will be survivable, which is the most common cause of post-handover complaint.
What goes on it: Ceiling and wall treatments, partition ratings, masking, planning-level separation.
Optional inputs: NRC and STC ratings; acoustic zoning plan
Notes: Escalates to mandatory under Industrial/Raw, where exposed soffits remove the usual absorption.

Purpose: Show that people can find their way without being escorted.
What goes on it: Signage family, hierarchy, typography, materials, key locations on plan.
Notes: Escalates on large floor plates and anywhere the public is received.

Purpose: Use the walls to say something specific about this company rather than a stock motivational line.
What goes on it: Graphic locations, content themes, the story each wall carries, materials.
Optional inputs: Content plan; heritage or archive material
Notes: Content sourcing is usually the bottleneck. Name who supplies it and by when.

Purpose: Show the planting as a designed, maintained system rather than pots added at handover.
What goes on it: Species by condition, planter design, locations on plan, irrigation and maintenance.
Notes: Mandatory under the Biophilic concept. Always state who maintains it and how often.

Purpose: Show the commissioned pieces, which at flagship grade carry much of the identity.
What goes on it: Pieces and locations, artists, commissioning approach, budget allocation.
Notes: Luxury flagship and Heritage projects. Commissioning lead times are long — put them on the programme.

Purpose: Fix the two largest continuous surfaces, which set the acoustic and maintenance baseline.
What goes on it: Ceiling systems and heights by zone, floor finishes by zone, transitions.
Notes: Heights per zone matter more than the finish. Show them where the plate is tight.

Purpose: Show that the detailing has been resolved, not left to the site to invent.
What goes on it: Key junction details: skirting, reveals, glazing, ceiling perimeter, joinery edges.
Notes: Premium and above, where the junction quality is most of what is being paid for.

Purpose: Mark the shift from appearance to performance.
What goes on it: Numeral, section title, framing question.

Purpose: Show the services are coordinated with the architecture rather than discovered to clash on site.
What goes on it: HVAC zoning, electrical distribution, plumbing, fire systems, ceiling coordination.
Notes: Name any base-build capacity shortfall explicitly. This is where late cost shocks originate.

Purpose: Fix what technology every room type gets, so nothing is negotiated room by room during delivery.
What goes on it: Room-type-by-room-type AV specification, display sizes, camera, audio, control.
Notes: Mandatory for GCCs — the parent's platform standard usually dictates it entirely.

Purpose: Show the infrastructure that everything else depends on.
What goes on it: Power distribution, data cabling, wifi coverage, UPS and server provision, charging.
Optional inputs: Server room specification; wifi heat map
Notes: Redundancy requirements belong here for GCC, BFSI and 24x7 operations.

Purpose: Show the sensing and booking layer, and be explicit about what it does with people's data.
What goes on it: Room booking, occupancy sensing, digital wayfinding, analytics, the privacy position.
Optional inputs: Platform selection; data and privacy policy
Notes: Occupancy sensing is a privacy conversation. Involve HR and Legal before it is specified, and say so here.

Purpose: Show compliance, because it can veto the plan and usually arrives late.
What goes on it: Egress routes and travel distances, detection and suppression, compartmentation, refuge.
Notes: If the circulation slide already carries egress distances, this slide can be short.

Purpose: Show the workplace works for everyone, and meets the standard it is held to.
What goes on it: Accessible routes, door widths, clearances, accessible washrooms and furniture, signage.
Notes: Name the standard being applied. 'Accessible' without a named standard is unverifiable.

Purpose: Show the access hierarchy, from public through staff to restricted.
What goes on it: Zones by access level on plan, control points, visitor management, CCTV coverage.
Notes: Mandatory for BFSI, R&D and GCC. Show it as a zoning overlay, not as a list.

Purpose: Show environmental performance as a design position rather than a disclaimer.
What goes on it: Material selection, energy and water strategy, reuse, waste and indoor health.
Notes: Escalates to mandatory under the Sustainable/Certified Green concept.

Purpose: Commit to a rating and show the credits that get there.
What goes on it: Target rating, credit scorecard, gaps, what the client must do and by when.
Notes: Certification changes programme and budget. Commit early or do not claim it at all.

Purpose: Mark the shift from design to money and time.
What goes on it: Numeral, section title, framing question.

Purpose: Show the number, broken down enough to be interrogated.
What goes on it: Cost by package — civil, joinery, MEP, furniture, AV, other — with totals and a contingency line.
Notes: GAP: no cost-table layout. title-stats handles 3-4 headline figures but not a full package breakdown.

Purpose: Give the one figure that travels — the number quoted in the meeting the client has after this one.
What goes on it: The figure, what it includes and excludes, and the benchmark band.
Optional inputs: Benchmark range; inclusions and exclusions list
Notes: Always state inclusions. A cost-per-seat without them is meaningless and will be misquoted.

Purpose: Surface the line items that actually move the number, rather than the whole schedule.
What goes on it: The top 10-15 lines by value, with quantity, rate and total.
Notes: GAP: no line-item table layout. SpaceBoq exists as a placeholder type only — the real table is unbuilt.

Purpose: Give the client levers to pull if the number is too high, before they start cutting arbitrarily.
What goes on it: Option, saving, and what is given up — so the trade-off is explicit.
Notes: GAP: no comparison-table layout. Always state what is lost; a saving without a cost reads as padding.

Purpose: Show when it will be finished and what has to happen for that to hold.
What goes on it: Phases from design through handover, with milestones, dependencies and the critical path.
Notes: GAP: no timeline or Gantt layout. merge-diagram shows sequence but neither duration nor overlap.

Purpose: Show who does what, and who the client calls when something goes wrong.
What goes on it: Team structure, roles, reporting lines, governance rhythm, escalation path.
Notes: Name the single point of contact. It is the thing clients most want from this slide.

Purpose: Show how the site will be run, which matters most where work happens in a live building.
What goes on it: Safety protocol, quality checkpoints, inspection regime, snagging process.
Notes: Escalates for refurbishment in an occupied building, and for plant-attached projects.

Purpose: Show what the client receives at handover and how the space is run afterwards.
What goes on it: Handover deliverables, O&M manuals, training, soft-landing period, facilities interface.
Notes: Mandatory for managed-office projects, where the operator has to run it from day one.

Purpose: State what is covered, for how long, and who to call.
What goes on it: Warranty periods by element, defects liability, response times, support contact.
Notes: Specific periods per element. A blanket '1 year warranty' invites disputes later.

Purpose: Put the assumptions in writing now, so a later change is a variation rather than an argument.
What goes on it: Key assumptions, risks with likelihood and mitigation, dependencies on the client.
Notes: The most under-used slide in the library and the one that saves the most money.

Purpose: Leave the room with a decision and a date rather than goodwill.
What goes on it: 3-5 actions, each with an owner and a date, and what is needed to proceed.
Notes: Owner and date on every line. A next-steps slide without both is a summary, not a close.

Purpose: Close cleanly, leaving contact details on screen through the Q&A.
What goes on it: Contact details, both logos, one closing image.
Notes: This slide stays up during questions — keep contact details legible from the back of the room.
